legend: Slava has a set of N$$$N$$$ numbers: x1,x2,x3,…,xn$$$x_1, x_2, x_3, \dots, x_n$$$. At one turn, he can get a non-empty set y1,y2,y3,…,ym$$$y_1, y_2, y_3, \dots, y_m$$$, in which for any i$$$i$$$ from 1$$$1$$$ to m$$$m$$$ yi$$$y_i$$$ is included in the set x1,x2,…,xn$$$x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n$$$, and then he can add in the set X$$$X$$$ sum of all products of numbers of all the possible subsets y1,y2,…,ym$$$y_1, y_2, \dots, y_m$$$. Slava is wondering: how many numbers not superior to L$$$L$$$ exist that can be calculated by the above-described method for the finite number of actions? (For better understanding, see the note).
input: The first line of the input data consists of numbers N$$$N$$$ and L$$$L$$$ (2≤N≤20,1≤L≤1012)$$$(2 \le N \le 20, 1 \le L \le 10^{12})$$$.
The second line consists of N$$$N$$$ numbers xi$$$x_i$$$ (2≤xi≤15)$$$(2 \le x_i \le 15)$$$.
output: In one line, output the number – the amount of numbers not superior to L$$$L$$$ that can be calculated by the above-described method for a finite number of actions.
note: Consider set of numbers X=[14,15],L=100$$$X = [14, 15], L = 100$$$.
We can get set Y$$$Y$$$ like that:
Among these numbers, only two are not superior to 100: 14, 15$$$100:~14,~15$$$.
